# Why the final section is about process

At an ICPC contest, knowing an algorithm is necessary but incomplete. A team
also loses time when two people silently work on the same idea, when a nearly
finished solution blocks the only keyboard, or when a wrong answer is followed
by random edits. The goal of this section is a process that preserves useful
thinking under time pressure.

This is not a claim that every regional has identical rules. Read your event's
rule sheet first. The local scoreboard drill defines the rule variant it uses.
The transferable habit is to turn the written rule into state before writing
code.

# The contest board is shared memory

Keep one visible row per problem:

```text
problem | owner | model claim | status | blocker | next test
```

The row should contain facts, not optimism. For example:

```text
F | Noor | bipartite matching, left=jobs right=machines | proof | capacity? | duplicate a machine by capacity
```

An owner has responsibility for the next decision. A reviewer may challenge
the proof, make a brute-force oracle, or prepare tests. This avoids the common
failure mode where two partial solutions exist and neither is ready to submit.

## A useful status vocabulary

| Status | Meaning | Next action |
|---|---|---|
| scan | statement read once | write a model candidate or risk |
| model | reduction is stated | check constraints and proof |
| proof | invariant or exchange argument is clear | code |
| coding | one owner uses the keyboard | reviewer produces tests |
| test | sample plus adversarial cases agree | submit |
| parked | no progress inside the time box | record the exact blocker |

`parked` is productive. It leaves a precise entry point for a teammate or for
your future self. `stuck` is not a useful status because it says nothing about
what information is missing.

# Triage is an estimate, not a promise

During the first 10--15 minutes, every teammate scans every problem. Give each
one a short card:

```text
known tool: 0-1 BFS
work estimate: 25 min
risk: state graph may be too large
first proof question: is every transition cost 0 or 1?
```

Choose work by expected *accepted* progress, not by alphabetical order or by
the problem that seems most interesting. A short implementation with a clear
proof is often a better first solve than a familiar but bug-prone geometry
task.

## Worked triage example

Suppose a team sees these cards:

| Problem | Estimate | Confidence | Risk |
|---|---:|---|---|
| A | 12 min | high | parsing |
| B | 28 min | high | overflow |
| C | 35 min | medium | endpoint convention |
| D | unknown | low | model absent |
| E | 40 min | high | long implementation |

One reasonable opening is `A`, `B`, and a second reading of `C`; park `D`.
This is not a rigid schedule. If the second reading reveals a one-line model
for `D`, update the board. The point is to make switching intentional rather
than accidental.

# The four-line pre-code contract

Before typing a medium or hard solution, the owner says or writes:

```text
model: graph whose nodes are (cell, direction)
invariant: dist[v] is the best discovered distance when popped from Dijkstra
complexity: O((V + E) log V), within the stated limits
tests: one cell, unreachable target, a zero-cost turn
```

This takes under a minute. It exposes gaps early: an owner who cannot name the
state probably should not start the implementation yet.

## Trace: a useful handoff

Poor handoff:

```text
"I tried G. It is probably DP."
```

Useful handoff:

```text
"G is DP on prefixes. dp[i] is the minimum cost after the first i items.
The transition needs the last chosen index, so the one-dimensional state is
not enough. My counterexample is [3, 1, 3]. Please check whether a deque can
keep the candidate minima."
```

The second version transfers the model, the failed assumption, and the next
experiment. A new owner can continue rather than reread the statement from
zero.

# One keyboard changes the workflow

When the keyboard is scarce, parallel work is still possible:

| Role | Concrete job |
|---|---|
| owner | writes the smallest correct implementation |
| reviewer | traces the proof, samples, and boundary cases |
| tester | writes a brute force or hand-crafted adversarial inputs |
| scout | refreshes problem cards and looks for newly recognized reductions |

Do not make roles permanent. Rotate after an accepted solution or a planned
handoff. The important rule is that keyboard time belongs to a solution with a
model and a test plan, not simply to the loudest unfinished task.

# Submission discipline

For the common scoring format, a wrong answer before an eventual acceptance
can add penalty. More generally, every submission costs attention and context.
Submit when the following checklist is true:

1. The code matches the stated model and invariant.
2. A teammate or your written trace checks the sample independently.
3. You tested the smallest legal input and the most dangerous boundary.
4. Integer types, indexing convention, and output format are explicit.
5. You know what result a failure would falsify.

This does not mean waiting for absolute certainty. It means making the risk
visible and testable.

## Scoreboard trace

For the local rule, a team gains a solved problem only on its first accepted
submission. The penalty for that problem is:

```text
accepted minute + 20 * wrong attempts before that acceptance
```

Consider submissions for team 2 on problem 4:

| Minute | Verdict | wrong attempts | solved | penalty contribution |
|---:|---|---:|---:|---:|
| 18 | W | 1 | 0 | 0 |
| 31 | W | 2 | 0 | 0 |
| 47 | A | 2 | 1 | 87 |
| 52 | W | 2 | 1 | 87 |

The final wrong answer does nothing because the problem was already solved.
Problem A turns this table into a reliable simulation.

# Time boxes and recovery

A time box prevents an invisible hour of low-information work. A reasonable
default is:

```text
10--15 minutes: no model -> park with an exact blocker
15--20 more minutes: model but no proof -> seek a reviewer
20 minutes of debugging: build a tiny oracle or switch bug category
```

When a submission fails, classify before changing code:

```text
parsing | model | proof | implementation | boundary | output format
```

For example, a failure only on `n = 1` points toward a boundary or indexing
issue; a failure on random tiny cases against a brute force points toward the
model or implementation. This classification chooses the next test.

# Train the workflow in stages

A five-hour virtual contest is valuable, but it is too large to diagnose a
single weak habit. Train the behaviors separately, then combine them. Repeat
this four-session loop with fresh problems from past ICPC-regionals or the
external queue in `PRACTICE.md`.

| Session | Format | Required artifact | What it isolates |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1. Solo model sprint | 75 min, 3 problems, no discussion | one four-line pre-code contract per problem | statement reading and algorithm selection |
| 2. Paired handoff | 90 min, 2 medium problems, one keyboard | a two-minute handoff note before every ownership change | state definition, proof communication, review |
| 3. Team sprint | 120 min, 4--5 problems under contest rules | shared board history and one classified test for each submission | triage, role rotation, submission discipline |
| 4. Full virtual | target contest length, target team and machine rules | final board plus a post-contest log | integration under realistic fatigue and time pressure |

The difficulty should rise across cycles, but the process does not change. A
team that cannot maintain a correct board in a two-hour sprint will not repair
that habit merely by extending the clock to five hours.

## Session 1: solo model sprint

Give each person three problems that are individually within reach. For each
problem, spend at most five minutes writing the model, invariant, complexity,
and two tests. Code only the clearest one first. At the end, compare the
contracts with the eventual editorials or an accepted solution, not just the
final answers.

Record two numbers:

```text
correct models before coding / problems read
minutes from first read to a precise model
```

These distinguish a recognition problem from an implementation problem. A fast
wrong model is not progress; a slow but precise model tells you what to train.

## Session 2: paired handoff

One person begins as owner. At a scheduled 20-minute mark, the partner must be
able to continue using only the board entry and a spoken two-minute handoff:

```text
state and invariant
what has been proved or tested
one counterexample, uncertainty, or blocker
the next action
```

The partner may reject the handoff if it lacks a state meaning or a falsifiable
next step. That is useful feedback, not a social failure. Swap roles once even
when the first owner could finish alone; practicing transfer is the point.

## Session 3: team sprint

Use the actual number of keyboards and prohibit silent duplicate
implementations. Every 25 minutes, pause for two minutes only to update the
board: owner, status, blocker, and next test. Do not conduct a new group solve
during the pause. This produces an audit trail of decisions without consuming
the whole sprint in discussion.

For every submission, preserve one test input and label its purpose:

```text
sample | smallest input | boundary | counterexample | random-oracle
```

After the sprint, inspect the first point where a wrong submission could have
been caught. Add that input to the team's regression folder or notebook.

## Session 4: full virtual and review

Run the full virtual with the target event's published rules. Keep the board,
but do not pause the clock. Within 24 hours, upsolve each unsolved problem for
a fixed 20 minutes before reading an editorial. Then write a one-line entry:

```text
problem | missing observation | first evidence that would reveal it | next drill
```

For example, `H | needed state (vertex, coupons_used), not vertex |
two coupons reaching the same vertex | state-expansion sprint` is actionable.
`H | hard DP` is not.

## Advancement criteria

Move from repeated sprints to frequent full virtuals only after two consecutive
team sprints meet all of these observable conditions:

1. Every active problem has an owner, a concrete status, and a next test.
2. Every ownership change includes a model and a blocker or counterexample.
3. Every wrong submission is classified and gains a regression test or a
   written reason why no small test can expose it.
4. Each teammate both owns a solution and reviews a different solution.

These are process criteria, not a required solve count. A team can solve fewer
problems and still improve sharply if its next virtual has fewer unforced
mistakes and faster recoveries.

# Three contest-operation algorithms

The exercises are intentionally familiar algorithmically. They test whether a
team can deploy known tools accurately when the statement is dressed as a
contest operation.

1. **Scoreboard Replay** is direct state simulation: each `(team, problem)`
   pair has a solved flag and a count of wrong attempts.
2. **Time-Boxed Schedule** is the deadline greedy from Section 9: retain a
   feasible set and remove its longest task when a deadline is exceeded.
3. **First-Round Assignment** is bipartite matching from Section 45: an edge
   means a teammate can own a problem in the initial parallel round.

## C++ notes

- Use a two-dimensional `vector` for scoreboard state; do not key it by a
  formatted string when team and problem ids are already bounded integers.
- Store penalties and elapsed time in `long long` even when the sample is
  small.
- `priority_queue<int>` is a max heap, exactly what the schedule greedy needs
  to remove the longest selected task.
- For matching, reset the right-side `seen` array for every DFS attempt.

## Python notes

- A nested list of booleans and integers makes the scoreboard state visible.
- `heapq` is a min heap, so push negative durations to remove the longest
  selected duration.
- Use recursion for tiny matching instances only when the recursion depth is
  comfortably bounded; iterative alternatives are safer for very large input.

# Local judge workflow

First run your stubs. They should fail until you implement them. Then verify
the reference solutions and use the random tests as a regression check:

```bash
python3 sections/61_icpc_contest_readiness/check.py
CP_TARGET=solution python3 sections/61_icpc_contest_readiness/check.py
```

For a solution with nontrivial logic, make one independent brute-force checker
before trusting random tests. A generator that asks the same algorithm for the
answer cannot reveal a shared mistake.

# Common mistakes

- Treating a first scan as a commitment to solve the problem.
- Letting multiple people independently code the same task without a reason.
- Handing off only a feeling instead of the current model and counterexample.
- Updating a scoreboard after submissions to an already solved problem.
- Removing the shortest, rather than the longest, task in the deadline greedy.
- Reusing matching `seen` marks across separate augmenting-path searches.

# Before you submit

```text
[ ] The board says who owns this submission.
[ ] I can state the model and invariant in one sentence each.
[ ] The complexity uses the actual maximum constraints.
[ ] A reviewer has traced a sample and a hostile tiny case.
[ ] I know the next test if this receives a wrong answer.
```

# Exercises

- A. Scoreboard Replay: simulate the stated ICPC-style scoring rules exactly.
- B. Time-Boxed Schedule: use a deadline greedy to maximize completed tasks.
- C. First-Round Assignment: model distinct initial owners as bipartite
  matching.
- D. Training-cycle retrospective: run one Session 2 or Session 3 drill from
  the table above. Preserve the board, one handoff note, and one test that
  would have prevented a real mistake. Convert the review into a single next
  drill rather than an unstructured list of topics.

# Contest checklist

State the model, invariant, complexity, and next test before the keyboard.
Record blockers precisely, park deliberately, and turn every post-contest
mistake into a future test or notebook warning.
